value: strongly attracted to water scented by zebra mussel in a two-choice fluviarium; no preference for water scented by fish (tilapia)
units: categorical (two-choice scent test; paired t-test P values)

source.authors: Matteo Rolla, Sofia Consuegra, Eleanor Carrington, David J. Hall, Carlos Garcia de Leaniz
source.title: Experimental evidence of chemical attraction in the mutualistic zebra mussel-killer shrimp system

method: behavioural: two-choice fluviarium, scented water (zebra mussel, Nile tilapia or blank) versus blank, paired t-tests
conditions: Wild-collected killer shrimp held in laboratory tanks at Swansea University; sympatric animals from Cardiff Bay and allopatric animals from Upper Mother Ditch (no zebra mussels). Scents: zebra mussels or tilapia held 24 h in dechlorinated water at 50 g/L biomass, delivered at 200 ml/min (tool summary). Experiment 3 tested blank versus tilapia scent and blank versus zebra mussel scent in each population. Results sentences read in abutting pieces: with tilapia scent 'no preference was observed over blank water, either in sympatry (t19 = 0.819, P = 0.423; Fig. 5C) or allopatry (t19 = - 0.687, P = 0.500; Fig. 5D)'; for zebra mussel scent, attraction in the sympatric (t27 = - 2.176, P = 0.038) and allopatric population (t19 = - 2.614, P = 0.017), no population difference (F1,118 = 1.036, P = 0.311, tool summary). Sample sizes do not reconcile in the page: Methods give 60 shrimp per population, figure captions 40 per scent treatment per population (tool summary). Scent strength is a prepared biomass dose; no concentration of chemical cues measured. The same paper's other experiments (settlement on mussel mats, not different from artificial grass) are not part of this value.
quote: Killer shrimp were strongly attracted to water scented by zebra mussel, but not to water scented by fish.

value: males visited capture webs spun by old females significantly more than webs of younger females, in trials with webs alone
units: categorical (male visits to webs; Fisher exact test)

source.title: Old maids have more appeal: effects of age and pheromone source on mate attraction in an orb-web spider

method: behavioural: field test of male attraction to a neutral web carrying a female's body or to the female's own web alone, three female age classes, two-hour trials, Fisher exact test
conditions: Females were collected as juveniles and sub-adults from a natural meadow near Nebenstedt, reared in the laboratory and tested in the field (Buxtehude, Lower Saxony, 12-26 July 2012; tool summary), so the females were wild-origin and the visiting males were free-living (Methods do not say where the males came from; males were released a few metres away after each test). Age classes young (1-2 days after maturation), middle-aged (3-7), old (8 or more); each female in one class. Web trials: 14 young, 14 middle-aged, 13 old (tool summary). Results read in abutting pieces: webs of old females (6 of 13 webs) 'attracted males significantly more often than webs of young females and webs of middle-aged females (for both pairwise comparisons we used the same statistic: N = 27, p = 0.0329, Fig. 1)'. Nulls from the same Results: a paired comparison of male visitors attracted by a given female in a neutral web and by her own web was not significant (Wilcoxon T = 58.5, N = 14, p = 0.3724). Only 23 of 77 tested females or webs were visited at all (tool summary). The compound responsible was not identified; attraction to a web is attributed to pheromone by the authors.
quote: Capture webs alone spun by old females were significantly more efficient in attracting males than webs of younger females.

value: bait taken in 33% of trials with the Scuba7 electric deterrent switched on versus 100% of trials with it off
units: percent of trials with bait taken

source.authors: Madeline Thiele, Johann Mourier, Yannis Papastamatiou, Laurent Ballesta, Eric Chateauminois, Charlie Huveneers
source.title: Response of blacktip reef sharks Carcharhinus melanopterus to shark bite mitigation products

method: behavioural: baited field trials with a commercial electric deterrent (Ocean Guardian Scuba7) randomly switched on or off in blocks of two, video scored single-blind, GLMM
conditions: Free-ranging blacktip reef sharks at Fakarava Atoll, French Polynesia, where locals feed the sharks daily, so the sharks were habituated to provisioning. Seven consecutive days in June 2017, 12 trials per day, status block-randomised before each set of two trials (Methods piece), 84 trials (42 on, 42 off) with 966 approaches (tool summary); trials up to three minutes. Results pieces: 'When the Scuba7 was inactive, sharks took the bait during all trials' and 'In contrast, sharks took the bait on 33% of the trials'; device status significantly affected all response variables (Table 1 not read). Also from tool summary: time to take bait 38.9 +/- 3.35 s (off) vs 165 +/- 20.40 s (on); approach distance 38.88 +/- 3.20 cm vs 80.98 +/- 1.72 cm. Electric field was modelled as a dielectric dipole; no measured field strength at the shark is reported for the trials. A second experiment (Kevlar-neoprene bite pouches) is not part of this value. The response is to a prepared deterrent next to bait, not a detection threshold.
quote: The Scuba7 reduced the proportion of baits being taken by 67%, (from 100% during control trials to 33%).
